spots.name: Fitzwilliam Museum
spots.label: Fitzwilliam Museum

text.access_note: The building can be photographed from the public pavement, and the museum is free to enter, with photography allowed inside without flash. It has been under restoration at times, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Trumpington Street in central Cambridge, where the museum stands opposite Fitzwilliam Street. From there the museum is just to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in central Cambridge on Trumpington Street, opposite Fitzwilliam Street.
text.description:
The Fitzwilliam Museum is the art and antiquities museum of the University of Cambridge, and its front is a formal, symmetrical classical facade. A tall classical portico with columns and a carved pediment sits above a broad flight of stone steps. It is a formal, symmetrical building, so it suits a simple straight-on photo.

The museum was founded in 1816 under the will of Richard FitzWilliam, 7th Viscount FitzWilliam. The main building, called the Founder's Building, was put up between 1837 and 1843 to designs by George Basevi, and C. R. Cockerell completed it. The carving, including the four lions, is by William Grinsell Nicholl. The museum opened in 1848, and the building and its street-front boundary are Grade I listed.

For your photo, cross Trumpington Street and stand on the far pavement opposite the main entrance. From there you can take in the whole portico and the entrance in one frame. Keep the phone level so the columns stay upright, and leave a little space around the building rather than cropping tight. If you want a people photo, the steps below the columns make a neat formal backdrop. Round the back, Coe Fen gives a quieter view of the rear of the museum. Check that angle on the ground, as it is less well known.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the portico up with the middle of the frame, keeping the columns vertical. Leave some space above the pediment and some pavement or railings at the bottom. For a more formal people photo, try the museum steps instead, with the columns rising behind. Coe Fen gives a quieter view of the rear of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural, front-on view of the portico. If the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole building in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the columns, pediment and lions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Trumpington Street (opposite the main entrance, across the road). The neoclassical portico and main entrance of the museum, framed straight on from the far pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the portico keeps its detail. If the ultra-wide makes the edges lean, step back and use the default lens (1x) instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Even, soft daylight, such as a bright overcast day or the morning, tends to suit the pale stone. Earlier in the day there are usually fewer people on the steps.

spots.name: Mathematical Bridge
spots.label: Mathematical Bridge

text.access_note: The view from Silver Street Bridge is from a public footpath, but the Mathematical Bridge itself is for Queens' College members and paying visitors only, so check the official site before you go if you want to visit the college.
text.directions_text: There are no nearby stations or tram stops, so head for Silver Street and Queens' College in the southwest of central Cambridge and walk to Silver Street Bridge. Stand on its public footpath. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In the southwest of central Cambridge, on the River Cam between two parts of Queens' College, about a stone's throw northwest of Silver Street Bridge.
text.description: The Mathematical Bridge is a small wooden footbridge across the River Cam that links two parts of Queens' College. It looks like a smooth arch, but it is built entirely from straight timbers, laid as a series of tangents and tied together with cross-pieces. That is where the name comes from, and it is why the bridge looks so neat in a photo: the criss-cross of timber shows up well against the water and the college buildings behind. The design is by William Etheridge, and James Essex built it in 1749. It has been rebuilt twice, in 1866 and 1905, but keeps the same shape, and it is Grade II listed. You may hear that Isaac Newton built it without bolts. He died over twenty years before it was built, so that story is a myth. The best-known photo is a side view from the footpath on Silver Street Bridge, looking upstream, with the wooden span in the middle and Queens' College behind. It is free to reach on foot, but it can get busy with other people taking the same picture, so be patient and take your turn at the rail. Keep your phone steady against the parapet, take a few frames, and wait for a gap if a punt drifts through. The bridge itself is not a free public crossing, so this view from the street is the easy way to see it.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up along one of the horizontal lines so the arch looks level. Leave a little water in the bottom of the frame. For a different angle, try Silver Street, at the street end, where boats passing through the scene add interest.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic side view of the whole bridge with the college behind it. If other people are in the way, switch to telephoto (2x or 3x) to pick out just the timber arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Silver Street Bridge (public footpath on the bridge, looking upstream toward the Mathematical Bridge). A wide classic view of the wooden bridge over the River Cam with Queens' College buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the timbers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the wood keeps its colour. Take a short burst or a Live Photo while a punt passes, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people.

spots.name: Queens' College
spots.label: Queens' College

text.access_note: Silver Street Bridge is a free public bridge, but the college itself may charge for entry and the Mathematical Bridge is reserved for college members, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Cambridge, head south towards Silver Street. Silver Street Bridge is a public bridge near the Mathematical Bridge, so check the map for its exact position. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: Queens' College is in the south of central Cambridge, on both banks of the River Cam, mostly on the east bank. It sits right beside Silver Street and the Mathematical Bridge.
text.description: Queens' College is one of Cambridge's oldest colleges, founded in 1448 by Margaret of Anjou and refounded in 1465 by Elizabeth Woodville. That double start is why the name has the apostrophe after the s. The college is one of only two whose main buildings straddle the River Cam, and the two halves are joined by the wooden Mathematical Bridge. The photo most visitors come for is that bridge arching over the water, with the college's old brick courts rising behind it. Often a punt slides underneath, which gives the picture a little life. The Old Court is described as one of the best-preserved medieval groups of buildings in the city, and the President's Lodge, from around 1460, is the oldest building on the river here. The bridge itself is reserved for college members, so visitors photograph it from outside rather than walking across. Silver Street Bridge is a free public bridge, and it lets you frame the whole arch from above without going into the college. For a quieter angle, try Queens' Road, which looks across the river to the same bridge from beside the Backs. Take a few frames in portrait and a few in landscape. The curve of the arch, the water and the brick all work well in either, and the reflections are worth including if the water is calm.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch along the lower third, leaving room for the brick courts above it. Wait for a punt to drift under the bridge before you press the shutter. If you want a calmer picture with fewer people in it, walk to Queens' Road and shoot across the river from there instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole arch of the Mathematical Bridge and the brick buildings behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the bridge parapet or other people crowd you in. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge and the old brick courts without moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Silver Street Bridge. The wooden Mathematical Bridge arching over the River Cam with the college's old brick courts behind it, often with a punt passing underneath. Check the map before choosing which side of the bridge to stand on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wooden bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the brick and timber keep their colour. A Live Photo can catch a punt moving through the frame, and you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is often calmer on the bridge, and softer daylight suits the brickwork. Any time works if you are patient for a punt to pass.
